title: One content contract
summary: Three layers that never merge, one typed schema, and blocks that reference widgets by id.

blocks.title: One content contract
blocks.body: Content changes words. Widgets change bones. Themes change skin. One change at a time.

columns.name: Content
columns.detail: What the idea says: sections, copy, links, data. No colors, no motion.

columns.name: Widgets
columns.detail: Pre-debugged building blocks: structure plus behavior. They own their layout and reduced-motion fallbacks.

columns.name: Themes
columns.detail: Tokens only: color, type, radius, spacing, motion intensity. They never redefine widget structure.

blocks.heading: A block references a widget by id

blocks.title: The rule that keeps it cheap
blocks.body: Copy-paste JSON content blocks that reference widgets by id - never widget code. Pasted widget code forks the widget. Bad CSS is cheap; fifty entries in five incompatible formats is expensive.

blocks.heading: The storage path
items: v0: content lives as plain JSON files next to the renderer.
The renderer only knows the content contract, never where content came from.
Later: another storage layer can back the same objects without changing the renderer contract.

blocks.heading: Spot the contract violation
blocks.prompt: A contributor wants one deck with a special animated banner. Which move respects the contract?
options: Paste a modified copy of the hero widget's code into the deck JSON
Request the capability in the renderer once, then reference it by id
Hide custom CSS inside the content file to force the look
blocks.explanation: Forked code and one-off CSS bypass the shared contract. A new capability is a renderer change, reviewed once, then available to every entry.

blocks.title: Architecture boundary
blocks.body: The renderer depends on the content contract, not a particular editor or storage system.

blocks.heading: Assembly, not debugging
blocks.body: Adding a page means adding a content file. No new routes, no per-page CSS, no forked widgets.
